Fellowlabourer
fĕl'ō-lā-bər-ər
n. (one who labours together with another in the gospel; Paul's ordinary title for those who worked beside him)
English fellow, a companion or partner, with labourer. The Greek sunergos is a compound — one who works together — and Paul uses it of men, of women, and once of himself and God.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Paul rarely calls anyone an assistant. He calls them fellowlabourers. Of Timothy: “And sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith” (1Th 3:2). Of the man who owned the runaway slave: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer” (Phm 1:1). At the close of the same short letter he names four more: “Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers” (Phm 1:24) — and one of those four would afterward forsake him, having loved this present world, which the apostle records without erasing the earlier commendation. Colossians calls a small group of Jewish believers “my fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me” (Col 4:11). And the highest use of the word makes the whole church a work-site under one Owner: “For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building” (1Co 3:9). The gospel is described throughout as labour — not a platform, not an office, but work done alongside other men.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives fellow-laborer as one who labors in the same business or design; and labourer as one who works, particularly one whose work requires bodily strength or constant application.

Key Scripture

1Th 3:2 — "And sent Timotheus, our brother, and minister of God, and our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ, to establish you, and to comfort you concerning your faith:"

Phm 1:1 — "Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, unto Philemon our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer,"

Phm 1:24 — "Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers."

1Co 3:9 — "For we are labourers together with God: ye are God's husbandry, ye are God's building."

Modern Corruption

Ministry has been reorganised around personalities and platforms, while the apostle's standing vocabulary for the work is a crew of men labouring together.

expand to see more

Paul's letters end in lists of names, and the lists are doctrine. He is the apostle to the Gentiles, he has seen the Lord, and he writes Scripture; and he calls a householder in Colosse his fellowlabourer and a young man from Lystra his brother and fellowlabourer in the gospel. There is a real and unrepeatable apostolic office in the New Testament, and the same New Testament shows that office surrounded by ordinary workers who are named, thanked and trusted with errands that mattered. Set beside that the arrangement now common, in which a ministry is built around one gifted man, his name on the building, his face on the material, and everyone else classed as staff or volunteers. The structure is not merely unwise; it contradicts the apostle's own account of how the work is done and who is doing it.

The list at Philemon 24 is worth reading slowly for a second reason. Demas is in it. In a later letter Paul writes that Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica — and the earlier commendation stands in the canon unaltered. Two things follow. The first is that a man may be a genuine fellowlabourer for years and afterwards go; profession is not perseverance, and the church is right to be sober about it. The second is that Paul does not retroactively deny the earlier labour or rewrite the record to protect himself from having endorsed a man who fell. That honesty is rare. Where a leader departs today, ministries commonly erase him from the history entirely, which is neither charitable nor truthful. Scripture's way is to name what was, name what happened, and leave both standing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sunergos (G4904), a fellow worker, from sun, together, and ergon, work; rendered fellowlabourer, fellowworker, and helper throughout the epistles.

expand to see more

Greek sunergos (G4904) — a fellow worker; used of Timothy, Philemon, Titus, Priscilla and Aquila, and of the church with God; 1 Thessalonians 3:2, Romans 16:3.

Greek ergon (G2041) — work, deed, labour; the root that makes ministry a trade rather than a title.

Greek kopos (G2873) — toil to the point of weariness; the labour of love which God is not unrighteous to forget; Hebrews 6:10.

Greek georgion (G1091) — a tilled field, husbandry; ye are God's husbandry; 1 Corinthians 3:9.

Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, minister; Timothy is minister of God and fellowlabourer in one clause; 1 Thessalonians 3:2.

Usage

"“Our fellowlabourer in the gospel of Christ” — the apostle's ordinary word for a colleague."

"“Marcus, Aristarchus, Demas, Lucas, my fellowlabourers” — and one of the four would go."

"“We are labourers together with God” — the work-site and its Owner."
